articles.title_orig: Wang urges China-US cooperation on AI development and governance
articles.title_zh: Wang urges China-US cooperation on AI development and governance
articles.content_orig:
China and the United States have both the capacity and the responsibility to work together on artificial intelligence development and governance, ensuring the technology remains under human control and benefits people, Foreign Minister Wang Yi said on Friday.
Wang made the remarks during a meeting with John L Thornton, co-chair of the Board of Trustees of the Asia Society, and New York Times columnist Thomas L Friedman in the Xiong'an New Area, Hebei province. Both were in China to attend the 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiong'an).
As two leading countries in AI, China and the US should cooperate not only to guard against risks but also to discuss globally applicable rules and standards, enabling the technology to promote shared prosperity and common security, Wang said.
China advocates inclusive AI development that serves the common good, he added.
On global governance, Wang said the world faced multiple deficits, including in peace, development and security. The Global Governance Initiative has provided an important public good and received broad international recognition and support, he said.
Wang praised Thornton and Friedman's longstanding efforts to promote China-US relations and expressed hope that they would contribute to the forum's success.
A press release issued by the Foreign Ministry quoted Thornton and Friedman as saying that the malicious use of AI posed the greatest risk to building a constructive US-China relationship of strategic stability. They expressed hope that the two countries would strengthen cooperation on the issue and provide an important public good for the world.
The international community was closely following the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting hosted by China, they said, expressing hope that China would use the occasion to play a distinctive and positive role in addressing global challenges.

articles.title_orig: Kim Jong Un Enters China via Dandong Bridge Ahead of High-Stakes Diplomatic Talks
articles.title_zh: Kim Jong Un Enters China via Dandong Bridge Ahead of High-Stakes Diplomatic Talks
articles.content_orig:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong via a newly opened bridge, according to South Korean officials.
The visit on Saturday comes about a week after the bridge linking the two countries was officially opened, 12 years after its completion, deepening economic ties between the Asian giant and its small, nuclear-armed neighbour.
Kim’s visit also comes a day before the anniversary of China joining the 1950–1953 Korean War.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang met Kim in the border city, the Reuters news agency said, quoting a South Korean official.
China’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Kim arrived in Dandong through the New Yalu River Bridge connecting the two countries, the Reuters and AFP news agencies reported, quoting unnamed South Korean government officials. South Korea’s Yonhap News Agency also reported the visit, citing an unidentified government source.
Analysts say the visit represents part of Kim’s increasingly assertive foreign policy, as he seeks to align Pyongyang with Beijing and Moscow in a united front against the United States under what he portrays as a “new Cold War”.
Experts said the opening of the New Yalu River Bridge, which stretches 3km (1.9 miles) across the Yalu River, was a key symbol of strengthening ties between the two countries and reflected their intent to expand trade. It is expected to accommodate two-way traffic around the clock, including container shipments and heavy cargo trucks.
The four-lane structure was completed in 2014, but its opening was delayed due to a lack of connecting roads and customs facilities on the North Korean side, according to South Korean news reports.
“The opening of the bridge has resolved a major bottleneck in China-North Korea trade logistics,” Lu Chao, an expert in China-North Korea relations at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, a Chinese government think tank in Shenyang, told Reuters.
“With the logistics constraint eased, bilateral trade is likely to increase further,” Lu said.
China is North Korea’s largest trading partner and a vital source of diplomatic, economic and political support for the reclusive state, although ties have not always been smooth.
China, which fought alongside North Korea in the Korean War, is Pyongyang’s main economic and diplomatic backer. However, North Korea has drawn closer to Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which analysts say has reduced Pyongyang’s reliance on Beijing.
Kim’s last known visit to China was in September 2025 to attend the 80th Victory Day celebrations in Beijing, where he held a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Xi made a state visit to North Korea in June in which he expressed Beijing’s willingness to expand bilateral cooperation in trade, agriculture, construction and technology, while Kim described ties with China as a top strategic priority.

articles.title_orig: Iran trying harder to target US personnel in Middle East, intelligence chief warns
articles.title_zh: Iran trying harder to target US personnel in Middle East, intelligence chief warns
articles.content_orig:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.
The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East , and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.
The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent.
Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.
Axios was first to report on the memo.
The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported.
"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a U.S. official told CBS News on Friday. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official also told CBS News this week that the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats.
Houthi militants have stepped up drone and missile attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeting oil infrastructure and airports. One strike on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport earlier this month killed at least a dozen people , including a U.S. citizen, and injured hundreds more.
Last weekend, U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries warned Americans to exercise caution due to Houthi attacks.
Although the U.S. and Iran have refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, President Trump has not ruled out restarting hostilities after next month's midterm elections. Iran has also continued to take responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
At a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump suggested the U.S. could launch another operation against Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement.
"We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," the president said, invoking the name of the U.S. military campaign launched in February.

articles.title_orig: Paris shuts museums and police deploy in big numbers for new protests across France
articles.title_zh: Paris shuts museums and police deploy in big numbers for new protests across France
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
The Louvre is closed on Saturday, along with several other major Paris museums, because of concerns about potential violence during planned protests , France 's culture ministry says.
The Orsay and Picasso museums are also among those that are closed, the ministry said.
The ministry called on all institutions under its authority to adopt any necessary measures to ensure “visitor safety, staff protection and the preservation of artworks”.
The closures follow protests last Saturday that descended into mayhem, with rioters setting fires, smashing shop windows, looting and clashing with police.
The clashes and widespread looting over the weekend marked France's most violent unrest in years, and the French capital has been gripped by social tension.
Art Basel Paris is among those taking the same tack.
After two days when admission was invite-only, the fair opened to the public on Friday – but only for the day.
Organisers cancelled the weekend program on Thursday, prompted by the threat of unrest.
The fair's Paris venue, the Grand Palais, is hosting 211 international galleries and their exhibitions for Art Basel, considered one of the world's most prestigious contemporary art fairs.
“It’s kind of like the art Olympics,” New York-based artist Drake Carr, who is showing his work with Mariposa Gallery, said.
A protest on Thursday afternoon in Paris was peaceful, and Art Basel's organisers announced the decision to close for the weekend around the same time.
The protest planned for Saturday is expected to be much larger.
"This decision has not been taken lightly, and the safety of everyone involved in the fair remains our utmost priority," organizers said in a statement.
Its website posted a similar announcement and said that weekend ticketholders would be contacted.
Saloni Doshi, an art collector who travelled to Paris from India for the fair, grew worried last Saturday as she saw the fires and panicked people.
She received phone calls from friends asking whether Paris was safe.
She agreed with the organisers' rationale to close.
“It's hard that something like this has to happen, but state activities and people's freedom have to continue,” she said.
“I cannot imagine that a bunch of elite, privileged people getting inconvenienced because of this should have a voice.”
Antoine Donzeaud and Elisa Rigoulet, the owners of the gallery exo exo, felt the same.
“We understand this decision, which we consider reasonable and consistent with the urgency of the social demands currently unfolding in France,” they said in a text message.

articles.title_orig: Suspect arrested after fire "completely engulfed" Hitler's Eagle's Nest mountain retreat in Germany
articles.title_zh: Suspect arrested after fire "completely engulfed" Hitler's Eagle's Nest mountain retreat in Germany
articles.content_orig:
A suspect has been detained in Germany following a fire at Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, known as Eagle's Nest, German police said.
Authorities were alerted to a fire at the Nazi leader's mountain residence on the peak of Obersalzberg at approximately 9:15 p.m. local time on Friday, Upper Bavaria South police said in a statement.
The building, also known as Kehlsteinhaus, was "completely engulfed in flames" when firefighters arrived, police said, but no one was found inside and there were no injuries reported.
Fire trucks had some difficulty accessing the site "due to the local conditions," authorities added.
"Shortly after the fire broke out, a suspect came into the focus of investigators," the statement said, adding that the cause of the fire is now under criminal investigation and one person was taken into custody.
At an elevation of 6,017 feet, Hitler's Eagle Nest was completed in 1938 and occasionally used by the Nazi leader as a temporary seat of government. The site was spared from Allied bombing during World War II, largely preserving its original state.
Since then, it has become a popular tourist attraction, which also operates as a restaurant and beer garden. According to its website, the Eagle's Nest is "one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hilter era" and it "stands for the insanity of the regime."

articles.title_orig: Gen Z are leading the European protests. Here’s why they’re angry
articles.title_zh: Gen Z are leading the European protests. Here’s why they’re angry
articles.content_orig:
The kids are not alright. Across Europe, young people are protesting issues ranging from a lack of funding for education to the cost of housing, posing massive challenges to governments already under pressure and providing a visible sign of the intergenerational frustration felt by Gen Z.
The precise configuration of these grievances is different in different countries. In Spain , the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her home served as the catalyst for this wave of protests; in France, it was students demonstrating in support of striking teachers; student protests have rocked Albania on and off for months, first sparked by plans for a luxury development backed by US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
Despite their different catalysts, however, all these movements have acted as a sort of black hole, drawing in any discontent before exploding in a catch-all outburst of frustration for a generation of young people who fear they won’t have the same opportunities as their parents. They have, in part, inspired each other, too. Protesters in Italy and Greece have referenced their French counterparts in their slogans. Housing protests in Spain spilled over into Portugal. And student unions across Europe are sharing advice and their experiences with one another, Alice de Brito, vice president of France’s main student union, UNEF, told CNN.
“I see so many more similarities than differences,” she said. “We are all talking about the need for investments in education, in the universities, in youth in general. But we are also talking about the cost of living, about housing.”
That echoes the demands made by Italian student union leader Sabrina Brizzola, who told a rally last weekend: “Let’s… make ourselves heard for schools that don’t collapse on our heads, for safe and dignified work, for public healthcare, for social justice.”
For Julius Fintelmann, the co-founder and editor-in-chief of the European Correspondent daily newsletter, the protests “reflect a kind of frustration, the feeling that Europe’s politics is failing to deliver for the next generation.”
As well as education and housing, he points to an increasingly uncertain job market, where artificial intelligence disproportionately affects entry-level jobs, and the climate crisis as laying the groundwork for this explosion of Gen Z anger. “I think fundamentally what we see is this promise that liberal democracy had, which was that the next generation will enjoy a better life than the current one, that promise simply doesn’t hold true anymore,” he told CNN.
And the European Union countries most affected by protests – Greece, Italy, France, Belgium, Spain and Portugal – share a gloomy economic backdrop and high levels of national debt, making it hard to increase public spending. Bond yields in France, for example, ticked up to their highest levels since 2002 on Wednesday, exerting more pressure on government budgets.
Student protests like this have been held at the start of the French school year in September and October for the past nine years as young people returning to education realize they don’t have enough teachers or good equipment, noted de Brito.
This year, however, they snowballed, as students demanded reduced class sizes, increased spending on teachers, investment in infrastructure to withstand the climate crisis and an end to police violence against young people. “People are just tired of waiting for an answer,” de Brito said.
Education is a theme that cuts across Europe’s borders. Thousands of students and teachers marched across Greece, including a group who gathered outside parliament in Athens chanting, “from Greece to France, we want public, free education,” according to Reuters. When students first occupied a high school in Rome, on October 7, they wrote “like in France” in the first line of the statement defending their actions.
The Italian government has sought to downplay any similarities with the protest movement in France. “The situation in Italy is very different from France,” Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said earlier this month, repeating a far-right claim that the French protests are fueled by the difficulty, absent in Italy, of integrating second-generation migrants into the school system.
Nonetheless, housing is another issue that cuts across national borders. Italian protesters say they have closely watched housing protests in Spain, which erupted in earnest in September and ultimately forced the government to call snap elections.
Students at a protest camp in Rome told CNN that affordable housing was inseparable from a good education. One, Elisa Pastore, said she and her brother can “barely” afford the rent for their shared room in Rome, where they attend university. For the first half of her degree, until her brother started university too, she had to commute 120 kilometers (75 miles) from outside Rome in order to save money.
Other groups are protesting, too. A blockade by truckers in Italy, outraged by the rising cost of fuel following the Iran war, has halted production of buffalo mozzarella and some pasta. And issues like housing transcend generational divides, drawing older generations into the protests as well.
In Portugal, thousands of people have gathered in Rossio Square, one of Lisbon’s busiest plazas, every evening this week. Some even pitched tents and 55 people were arrested in the early hours of Tuesday morning, prompting further demonstrations. Protesters, waving flags with slogans like “Casas para morar,” meaning “Homes to live in,” have demanded caps on rent hikes and the reversal of a new law that would make evictions easier.
Elsewhere, long-running demonstrations in Albania and Serbia have focused more on anti-corruption, spiraling into movements seeking to topple each country’s government.
After the protests in Albania turned violent last week, Prime Minister Edi Rama resisted any calls to step down, instead accusing protesters of threatening his plans for the country to join the EU and blaming his political opponents for the unrest.
“We want a change, that’s why we’re here,” one protester in Albania told Reuters. “We want a revolution, we want a new government, we are not looking for any negotiations, we need a new government as soon as possible.”
Meanwhile in Serbia, the student-led protests that have shaped the country’s politics for the past two years now form the most formidable opposition to longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in parliamentary elections on Sunday.
More demonstrations are likely to come. Two of France’s biggest trade unions have called for further protests in Paris on Saturday, though French President Emmanuel Macron has moved to ban “illegitimate” protests, meaning only those linked to trade unions will be allowed by authorities. Nonetheless, widespread demonstrations are expected in Orléans, where hard-right figurehead Marine Le Pen launches her presidential campaign this weekend.
Major trade unions in France and Spain have called for a general strike on November 5 and 11, respectively. In Germany, a group calling itself “Gen Z regelt” (“Gen Z’s got it”) has called for nationwide protests on October 31. And student unions in Britain and Italy are planning a day of action on November 20 to protest the rising cost of education.
CNN’s Stefano Pozzebon, Pierre Bairin, Lucie Lepellec and Will Ripley contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: 61 Switch 1 & 2 Games You Should Check Out In Nintendo's 'Halloween Sale' (Europe)
articles.title_zh: 61 Switch 1 & 2 Games You Should Check Out In Nintendo's 'Halloween Sale' (Europe)
articles.content_orig:
After Nintendo of America launched its ' Screaming Deals ' sale earlier this week, we knew it wouldn't be long before Europe followed suit.
The 'Halloween Sale' is now live for those in Europe, with delicious discounts on a boatload of titles available until 1st November . So, naturally, we have assembled the following list to make things a little more manageable.
Below, you will find every game in the Halloween Sale that we rated a 9/10 or higher, plus a personal pick from all the games that fall below this review bar. We've listed things alphabetically and given the discounted price, so you know what you're paying for each.
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 854k
As ever, if you're looking to grab some eShop credit before diving in, we've got you covered with the following links from our store .
Please note that some external links on this page are affiliate links, which means if you click them and make a purchase we may receive a small percentage of the sale. Please read our FTC Disclosure for more information.
Alien: Isolation is a survival horror masterpiece and straight-up one of the very best horror video games ever released.
It's a nerve-wracking affair — a slow, methodical game of cat and mouse against a brilliantly clever recreation of one of cinema's most infamous killers — but if you're up to the task you'll find one of the most satisfying gameplay experiences in the genre; a brilliant and beautiful homage to one of the greatest sci-fi movies of all time.
Feral Interactive has done a stellar job with this Switch port and the excellent motion controls and inclusion of all previously-released DLC only go to sweeten the deal. This is essential stuff for survival horror fans.
Developer Shared Memory's stated goal was “to craft complete experiences that will be playable long after the world loses its internet connection,” and screen after screen, Animal Well excels in delighting your eyes and giving your brain something to stew on.
It’s a riposte against a culture of post-launch updates in favour of a meticulously crafted, singular vision with potentially years’ worth of discoveries baked in. By all indications, Animal Well delivers on that long-term promise and does so with a one-of-a-kind elegance.
BlazBlue CentralFiction Special Edition may have arrived a few years late on Switch, but that delay didn't dull the sharpness of its 2D fighting package.
Not only does it give the Ragna saga a proper send-off with a story mode that's so rich in character development it could be a full anime season in its own right, but it offers a staggering number of modes to keep you playing long after the credits roll. It runs silky-smooth docked or in handheld modes and runs like a dream online.
The lack of an English dub still rankles, and new adopters are going to have to do a lot of research to understand what's going on, but it's well worth the effort.
BlazBlue: Cross Tag Battle is an utterly accomplished 2D fighting game. It's bursting with content and featuring the visual spectacle of combat that uses up every single trick in the book. A few strange decisions aside, this title is a must for fighting game fans.
Even if you're not a fan of any of the franchises represented in this game, you most certainly will be by the time you're done with this stacked fighting package.
If Blue Prince were only about finding Room 46 and nabbing your inheritance, it would be a neat little puzzler with some fun twists along the way. For those who dive in headfirst and keep track of everything else it throws at you, however, it is so much more than that.
Rarely has a game made us feel more clever, more lost, and more elated the deeper into it we ventured, and still some question marks remain over its deeper mysteries. Minor technical drops and a lack of cross-save aside, this remains a superb achievement and one of the finest head scratchers we've had the pleasure of playing.
It looks like The Witness and it plays a bit like StreetPass Garden , but Botany Manor blooms into something that's not only entirely its own, but also something quite special. Don't let its cosy aesthetics fool you — Botany Manor is packed with nicely challenging, well-designed puzzles, and isn't afraid to tackle heavy subjects, too.
Chained Echoes is a wonderful mash-up of '90s JRPG tropes, masterfully woven together to produce an experience that feels simultaneously nostalgic and fresh. A well-paced story, unconventional progression system, tactical combat system, and expansive world all come together to make for a game that is shockingly one of the very best RPGs that we played in 2022.
Really, there’s no place where it feels like Chained Echoes drops the ball, which is all the more impressive when you consider that the vast majority of it was put together by one person. It stands as a shining example of everything that makes RPGs great.
As an adventure game, Chicory: A Colorful Tale is quite sincerely up there with the very best of the genre.
There’s plenty to see and do and a full completion run will probably take you 25-30 hours. The characters and their travails are rich and likeable, the game’s sense of humour is generally inspired, and it’s all very sweet without being sugary-twee and talking down to the player. It’s also an affecting little tearjerker that will definitely strike a chord if you make art, and almost certainly will even if you don’t – so long as you’re capable of pretty basic empathy.
Chicory is simple to play but impressively long and complex, with perfect controls, performance and visuals. Throw yourself into painting the world and you’ll be left with a game that’s very much your own and speaks to you directly – a beautiful marriage of mechanics, themes and visuals.
While it’s a shame that there are fewer games here than in other Konami collections — we’d have loved to have seen NES title Contra Force or the now-extinct WiiWare title Contra ReBirth — the ones included in the Contra Anniversary Collection are universally brilliant. The 8-bit and 16-bit Contra games are among the finest examples of the run ‘n gun genre, and to have almost all of them included in a single release and emulated flawlessly is an absolute treat.
Whether you’re a fan of the series or a curious onlooker who’s always wanted to see what the fuss was all about, this is essential.
We really like Crawl , and we’d bet our collected stash of gold and wrath you will, too. A dungeon-crawling hack-and-slash affair with roguelike elements, one player is the hero trying to get through a dungeon and the others play as monster-controlling ghosts attempting to kill said hero and take their place.
It's an everyone-for-themselves free-for-all, yet there are opportunities for frantic 3v1 co-operative play — a necessity when all the non-hero ghost characters must take joint control of bosses the hero faces. It’s great fun in single-player thanks to some aggressive AI, but that consistent danger takes on a new dimension when you and three of your friends are jostling for XP and that all-important killing blow.
Competitive couchplay doesn’t get much better than this on Switch.
A roguelike at heart with a rhythm-game soul, Crypt Of The NecroDancer is a sublime experience that’s a must-play for fans of the genre(s).
Its upbeat, uptempo take on dungeon crawling is infectious, and there’s enough content here to last even the savviest of spelunkers for many, many dance-fuelled dives into the depths. If you’ve never tangoed with the NecroDancer, this fully-featured Switch edition is the perfect way to jump in.
For anybody who never played this but loved the Zelda spin-off Cadence of Hyrule and was left wanting more, what are you waiting for?

This year, however, they snowballed, as students demanded reduced class sizes, increased spending on teachers, investment in infrastructure to withstand the climate crisis and an end to police violence against young people. “People are just tired of waiting for an answer,” de Brito said.
Education is a theme that cuts across Europe’s borders. Thousands of students and teachers marched across Greece, including a group who gathered outside parliament in Athens chanting, “from Greece to France, we want public, free education,” according to Reuters. When students first occupied a high school in Rome, on October 7, they wrote “like in France” in the first line of the statement defending their actions.
The Italian government has sought to downplay any similarities with the protest movement in France. “The situation in Italy is very different from France,” Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said earlier this month, repeating a far-right claim that the French protests are fueled by the difficulty, absent in Italy, of integrating second-generation migrants into the school system.
Nonetheless, housing is another issue that cuts across national borders. Italian protesters say they have closely watched housing protests in Spain, which erupted in earnest in September and ultimately forced the government to call snap elections.
Students at a protest camp in Rome told CNN that affordable housing was inseparable from a good education. One, Elisa Pastore, said she and her brother can “barely” afford the rent for their shared room in Rome, where they attend university. For the first half of her degree, until her brother started university too, she had to commute 120 kilometers (75 miles) from outside Rome in order to save money.
Other groups are protesting, too. A blockade by truckers in Italy, outraged by the rising cost of fuel following the Iran war, has halted production of buffalo mozzarella and some pasta. And issues like housing transcend generational divides, drawing older generations into the protests as well.
In Portugal, thousands of people have gathered in Rossio Square, one of Lisbon’s busiest plazas, every evening this week. Some even pitched tents and 55 people were arrested in the early hours of Tuesday morning, prompting further demonstrations. Protesters, waving flags with slogans like “Casas para morar,” meaning “Homes to live in,” have demanded caps on rent hikes and the reversal of a new law that would make evictions easier.
Elsewhere, long-running demonstrations in Albania and Serbia have focused more on anti-corruption, spiraling into movements seeking to topple each country’s government.
After the protests in Albania turned violent last week, Prime Minister Edi Rama resisted any calls to step down, instead accusing protesters of threatening his plans for the country to join the EU and blaming his political opponents for the unrest.
“We want a change, that’s why we’re here,” one protester in Albania told Reuters. “We want a revolution, we want a new government, we are not looking for any negotiations, we need a new government as soon as possible.”
Meanwhile in Serbia, the student-led protests that have shaped the country’s politics for the past two years now form the most formidable opposition to longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in parliamentary elections on Sunday.
More demonstrations are likely to come. Two of France’s biggest trade unions have called for further protests in Paris on Saturday, though French President Emmanuel Macron has moved to ban “illegitimate” protests, meaning only those linked to trade unions will be allowed by authorities. Nonetheless, widespread demonstrations are expected in Orléans, where hard-right figurehead Marine Le Pen launches her presidential campaign this weekend.
Major trade unions in France and Spain have called for a general strike on November 5 and 11, respectively. In Germany, a group calling itself “Gen Z regelt” (“Gen Z’s got it”) has called for nationwide protests on October 31. And student unions in Britain and Italy are planning a day of action on November 20 to protest the rising cost of education.
CNN’s Stefano Pozzebon, Pierre Bairin, Lucie Lepellec and Will Ripley contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: El Salvador sends special forces to search for troops missing in Haiti
articles.title_zh: El Salvador sends special forces to search for troops missing in Haiti
articles.content_orig:
El Salvador has deployed troops to Haiti to try to rescue four Salvadoran service members believed to have been captured by Haitian gangs, according to a spokesperson for the UN-authorized multinational security mission in Haiti known as the Gang Suppression Force (GSF).
The missing service members, described as non-combatant aviation technicians that were supporting the GSF mission, were ambushed by gangs on October 18, Salvadoran officials have said.
The GSF has been carrying out a dayslong operation to try to find them. The effort has resulted in armed clashes that have left at least seven gang members dead and four GSF personnel wounded, the GSF has said.
A spokesperson for the security mission confirmed to CNN on Thursday Salvadoran troops had arrived in Haiti to support the effort.
The Miami Herald first reported that a 100-strong team was deployed. El Salvador has not commented on the specific details of the mission.
It comes a day after Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele announced that his country had launched an unspecified “military operation” to rescue the missing men.
Can hired mercenaries succeed where others have failed?
Bukele, who has carried out a brutal crackdown on gangs in his own country, warned Haitian gang members that they would face a more severe response if they didn’t release the service members alive.
“And do not take our word for empty threats. We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too,” he said on X.
Gang leader Lanmo Sanjou issued a response to Bukele on Thursday, filming himself with large quantities of ammunition and warning that his group would “fight to stay alive.”
The GSF was established by the UN Security Council in 2025 to help Haiti fight the gangs plaguing the country . According to the resolution adopted at that time, the force consists of 5,500 military or police personnel and 50 civilians from various nations. El Salvador is one of the countries that agreed to provide personnel. Bukele says their primary job is to carry out medical evacuations.
CNN’s Mauricio Torres contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Iran Plots, Houthi Attacks Spur US Departure Orders in Mideast
articles.title_zh: Iran Plots, Houthi Attacks Spur US Departure Orders in Mideast
articles.content_orig:
Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target US personnel" in the Middle East and other areas, the US national intelligence director has warned in a memo seen by the BBC.
Jay Clayton's assessment come as the US State Department makes adjustments to staffing at diplomatic posts in the region, including the ordered departure earlier this week of non-emergency US embassy staff from Saudi Arabia.
The order came in response to escalating attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis against Saudi Arabia in the past month.
Clayton's memo was marked unclassified and sent to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday.
It said: "The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries."
Clayton said he was making every effort to downgrade as much intelligence as possible so Rubio could share it with US State Department personnel.
A US official told the BBC: "When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment.
"The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting US officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
At least 21 people have now been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities.
One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others – the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
The Houthis say the attacks on Saudi Arabia are in retaliation to what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport they blame on the kingdom.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks. Some 155 civilians have been killed in Yemen since, according to the Houthi-run health ministry.
This particular conflict has re-emerged on the backdrop of a wider conflict in the Middle East.
The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.
In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
The situation in the Strait of Hormuz has seen oil prices surge, exacerbated by the Houthis' "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia.

articles.title_orig: Attack in the West Bank kills 2 Israeli soldiers, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Attack in the West Bank kills 2 Israeli soldiers, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
Benjamin Netanyahu and ministers promise demolitions and forced displacement after deadly gunfight
Israel has launched a campaign of collective punishment against Palestinians in Hebron after gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers and injured three near a checkpoint outside the city.
Benjamin Netanyahu announced a siege on Hebron and neighbouring Halhul and said residents of the gunmen’s home neighbourhoods would all be forced out. He promised mass demolitions of homes.
The first destruction began within hours of the attack, as ministers who had been on the campaign trail ahead of elections on Tuesday rushed to the site of the shooting.
The far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, posted a video of himself in front of a bulldozer as it tore down a Palestinian home near the site of the firefight.
The destruction of a home built without permits aimed to “create deterrence and exact a price”, Smotrich said. There was no claim of a connection between the building’s owners and the attackers.
Soon after the destruction began, Israel’s high court issued a temporary order to stop the demolitions. A human rights lawyer, Mohammed Dahleh, filed an urgent petition on behalf of two factory owners nearby, arguing that the demolition violated international law on collective punishment and Israeli administrative law.
“What we saw today was an attempt to copy the illegal practices used in Gaza, in the heart of the West Bank ,” Dahleh said. “They want to wipe out entire areas exactly as they did in Gaza and the refugee camps in the West Bank.”
Michael Sfard, a leading Israeli lawyer, said Smotrich’s video was a “direct admission” that the demolitions were a collective punishment. He noted that deterrence had been used as an excuse for collective punishment since antiquity.
The defence minister, Israel Katz, promised further mass demolitions and forced displacement. He drew an explicit comparison with Gaza and said Hebron would be targeted in the same way as Jenin refugee camp, where nearly 20,000 people have been forced from their homes. Hebron is the largest Palestinian city in the occupied West Bank, with about 250,000 residents.
Katz said: “The Jenin refugee camp model arrives in Hebron. Every clan neighbourhood in Hebron from which the terrorists emerged today will be evacuated of its residents. Just like in Gaza, just like in Lebanon.”
Netanyahu announced that plans had been drawn up for the largest military operation in the West Bank since 1967, when Israeli forces occupied the Palestinian territory and forcibly displaced about 300,000 Palestinians.
No date had been set “but it is on the way”, he said in a statement that also pledged mass forced displacement and demolitions in Hebron and the expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
The attack was launched by two men armed with an assault rifle and a handgun, according to the Israeli military. The men, who were driving a car with Israeli number plates, opened fire after they were stopped by soldiers at a temporary checkpoint outside Hebron. They were killed after a 20-minute gunfight.
An AFP photographer who was on the way to another assignment and witnessed the gun battle saw two Palestinian men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle exchanging fire with Israeli forces.
Prominent Israelis, including a candidate for the far-right Amcha Yisrael party, shared conspiracy theories groundlessly accusing the AFP photographer of links to the gunmen after he documented the Hebron attack.
The Foreign Press Association (FPA) said it was deeply alarmed by claims the photographer had been tipped off, describing them as “dangerous and defamatory”. “He is a longtime professional who was on his way to another assignment and courageously documented what he saw in keeping with his professional duties,” the FPA said in a statement.
The incident came a week after settlers severely injured the photographer Heidi Levine as she documented attacks on Palestinians attempting to harvest olives in the occupied West Bank. Israel has also denied entry to several European journalists and an academic.
Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion, ethnic cleansing and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.
Attacks have intensified further since the start of the annual olive harvest in late September. Israeli settler militants have used violence to stop Palestinians bringing in a crop that is economically and culturally vital to their communities.
Israel holds elections on Tuesday. The current far-right coalition, which backs settlers politically and financially, is seeking to shore up voter support in the face of polls that show it is likely to loose its majority.
Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right national security minister, also travelled to Hebron on Friday and demanded the dismantling of the Palestinian Authority and restrictions on Palestinians’ freedom of movement, which is already heavily curtailed by Israeli controls, checkpoints and roadblocks.

articles.title_orig: Typhoon Champi kills one and injures more than 500 in Taiwan as it heads to China
articles.title_zh: Typhoon Champi kills one and injures more than 500 in Taiwan as it heads to China
articles.content_orig:
Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled
Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.
Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).
The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.
Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan .
Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.
Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.
Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.
Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.

articles.title_orig: US is reducing staffing at 4 Middle East embassies over increased threats from Iran
articles.title_zh: US is reducing staffing at 4 Middle East embassies over increased threats from Iran
articles.content_orig:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.
The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East , and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.
The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent.
Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.
Axios was first to report on the memo.
The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported.
"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a U.S. official told CBS News on Friday. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official also told CBS News this week that the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats.
Houthi militants have stepped up drone and missile attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeting oil infrastructure and airports. One strike on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport earlier this month killed at least a dozen people , including a U.S. citizen, and injured hundreds more.
Last weekend, U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries warned Americans to exercise caution due to Houthi attacks.
Although the U.S. and Iran have refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, President Trump has not ruled out restarting hostilities after next month's midterm elections. Iran has also continued to take responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
At a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump suggested the U.S. could launch another operation against Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement.
"We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," the president said, invoking the name of the U.S. military campaign launched in February.

articles.title_orig: FBI takes over investigation into cards stolen from FedEx truck outside PSA headquarters
articles.title_zh: FBI takes over investigation into cards stolen from FedEx truck outside PSA headquarters
articles.content_orig:
SANTA ANA, Calif. (KABC) -- Nearly $1 million in rare trading cards, including highly valued Pokémon cards, were stolen from a FedEx truck parked near an Orange County business that authenticates and grades the collectible items, according to police.
The theft is the latest in a string of heists involving Pokémon cards, which have exponentially increased in value in recent years.
The Santa Ana Police Department said in a statement on Tuesday that the heist occurred on Oct. 13 outside the Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA) office in Santa Ana.
The hundreds of stolen cards are estimated to be worth a total of $963,000, according to police.
"However, the exact value of the stolen items has not yet been determined," according to the Santa Ana police statement.
The cards belong to collectors from across the country who submitted them to the PSA to be authenticated and graded.
Two full pallets of collectible cards were stolen, and some cards on a third pallet were also swiped when thieves broke into a FedEx truck, according to police.
"The pallets contained various trading cards, including, but not limited to, sports cards and Pokémon cards," according to the police statement.
Thieves carve hole through drywall to steal high-value Pokémon cards from Anaheim shop
As of Wednesday, no arrests have been announced in the memorabilia rip-off. Police said the investigation is ongoing.
"The value is definitely there," said Gregory Lawrence of Shiny Vault Pokémon Cards. "It's another asset class now. It's not just stocks, bonds, and putting money in the bank. You can put money into cards. Whether it's Pokémon or sports, there is a huge following from across the world."
The theft was first reported by The Athletic, which cited police sources saying the the FedEx truck was broken into during the 60 to 90 minutes the driver was away from the parked vehicle.
"We are aware of a theft involving a third-party shipping vehicle carrying PSA-graded items. We are working closely with law enforcement and the carrier as the investigation continues," Collectors, the parent company of PSA, said in a statement to ABC News.
The company said it deactivated the certificates for the missing cards and has notified its "marketplace partners to be on the lookout for rare and serialized items."
"Our customer service team has contacted affected customers directly and is arranging compensation based on fair market value," the company said. "We understand the impact this has on collectors involved, many of whom see these cards as far more than a financial asset."
FedEx released a statement to ABC7, saying, "The security of our customers' shipments is a top priority, and we are working with local law enforcement in their investigation. Further questions should be referred to local investigators."
One victimized collector, known by his online handle, Sky-B Cards, issued a YouTube video statement , saying the 104 cards he submitted to PSA for grading were among the stolen items. He said he paid more than $8,000 to have the cards graded by PSA and that his cards were insured for more than $150,000.
"These were 104 cards that I've accumulated over two years," Sky-B Cards said in the YouTube video. "There are many irreplaceable cards in here that I will never see again, and honestly that's what hurts the most, outside of being absolutely financially destroyed here."
The heist is the latest in a string of thefts in Southern California and elsewhere in the country of highly valued Pokémon cards, highlighting what appears to be an ever-growing demand for merchandise from the popular childhood card game.
In February, thieves broke into a collectibles shop in Anaheim, by cutting a hole through the wall from a neighboring shop they also broke into, stealing tens of thousands of dollars worth of Pokémon cards.
Captured on video surveillance cameras, the three thieves were seen grabbing hundreds of trading cards and bolting from the shop in less than 10 minutes.
In April, thieves staged a smash-and-grab heist at Elite Sports Cards in Chicago, stealing $100,000 in Pokémon cards, the store owner told ABC Chicago station WLS.
In an interview in April, Jared Mast, president of Mast Wealth Management Group, which deals in alternative investments including collectibles like Pokémon cards, told ABC News the value of Pokémon cards has risen sharply in the past year.
"I would say, collectively, over the last 12 months, things have gone up anywhere from 200 to 300%," Mast said.
Mast explained that Pokémon card value has risen in three different waves over the last decade. First, in 2016, with the arrival of Pokémon Go, the popular mobile game based on the playing cards, and then again in 2019 and 2020, as a generation of celebrities like Logan Paul invested in the collectibles.
ABC News contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Argentinian judge drops fraud investigation into Milei over crypto scandal
articles.title_zh: Argentinian judge drops fraud investigation into Milei over crypto scandal
articles.content_orig:
An Argentinian federal judge has dropped a criminal investigation into President Javier Milei and his sister Karina Milei over the collapse of a cryptocurrency he promoted online.
Judge Marcelo Martinez de Giorgi issued the decision on Friday, according to court records, ending an inquiry into Milei’s role in the launch of the $Libra token, which crashed after a brief rally.
“The reported events do not constitute a criminal offence,” the judge said in a ruling. He also wrote that investor losses and the rise and fall in the currency’s price were insufficient to establish fraud.
In his ruling, Martinez de Giorgi said that Milei’s institutional standing could have given the launch “greater impact” when he posted about it, but that does not translate into a fraudulent scheme.
Javier Milei recommended the little-known meme coin in a post on X in February 2025. He later deleted the post and denied any link to the cryptocurrency, whose value soon plunged.
The judge also dismissed an investigation into US businessman Hayden Davis, who described himself as a “launch adviser” for the token. Davis has acknowledged that he held close to $100m after the crash and denies any wrongdoing.
“For the first time in history, a President of the Nation was investigated with complete freedom, resulting in absolute proof of his innocence,” read a post shared on X by the official presidential office.
“The question that remains is this: Who will take responsibility for having wasted Argentine taxpayers’ money and the President of the Nation’s time in a failed attempt at an institutional coup?”
Milei is one of US President Donald Trump’s closest allies. Trump firmly backed him a year ago and has called him his “favourite president”.
Trump made clear the support hinged on a victory for Milei’s party.
“I’m with this man because his philosophy is correct,” he said ahead of a White House lunch with the Argentinian leader last year. “If he wins, we’re staying with him. And if he doesn’t win, we’re gone.”
Earlier this month, Milei urged Trump to emerge stronger from the US midterm elections, saying the vote mattered for the West as a whole.
Since taking office in 2023, Milei has laid off thousands of state employees , shut ministries, cut subsidies and reduced government-funded programmes. The measures were meant to fight high inflation, which has fallen to about 2 percent a month.
Milei says his plan is working, claiming that Argentina has grown for 27 consecutive months and is expanding at four times its historical rate.
When the coin crashed, Milei said he had acted “in good faith” and accused his political rivals of trying to exploit the situation.

articles.title_orig: Pentagon designates China-backed campus cultural centers a threat to US national security
articles.title_zh: Pentagon designates China-backed campus cultural centers a threat to US national security
articles.content_orig:
Defense secretary Pete Hegseth alleges Confucius Institutes operating in disguise on US university campuses
The ⁠US defense department has designated Chinese-funded cultural centers on university campuses ⁠known as Confucius ⁠Institutes ​as a threat to US national security, defense secretary Pete ⁠Hegseth said on Friday.
Washington has long accused Confucius Institutes of being Chinese propaganda ⁠tools and has taken steps to ​crack down on them.
Hegseth, ‌in a ‌video posted on social media, alleged that Confucius ‌Institutes were operating under disguise at US universities and that the Pentagon had added them to its list of institutions that threaten US national security.
“It turns ‌out that 80 new propaganda cells across 30 universities had popped ​up using different names and different charters, but with the same mission: to steal intellectual property and to infiltrate the minds ⁠of American students,” Hegseth said.
The defense department over ​the ​past two months has “systematically ​dismantled every single one of ​these organizations”, he ‌said.
The Chinese ​embassy ​in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: NASA Chief Warns China Is Closing Gap in ‘New Space Race’
articles.title_zh: NASA Chief Warns China Is Closing Gap in ‘New Space Race’
articles.content_orig:
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman warned Friday that the United States is in a "new space race" with China, saying that the agency must recapture the urgency of the Apollo era if it hopes to return astronauts to the moon first.
China launched its first astronaut in 2003, he said, and has since built up a broad portfolio of space capabilities, including lunar missions and plans for a crewed moon landing before 2030. These rapid advances have created a competition far closer than the Cold War race that culminated in the Apollo moon landings, Isaacman said, during an Artemis update at Kennedy Space Center in Merritt Island, Florida.
"Nor will NASA sit idly by and watch one of the most consequential moments of this new century pass to our overseas competitors," he said. "The appetite for tolerating and defending the status quo has reached its conclusion."
NASA reaffirmed its summer plans for Artemis III, and for Artemis IV—the mission scheduled to return astronauts to the lunar surface—in 2028. The agency will continue to depend on Elon Musk's SpaceX and Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin to achieve these goals.
According to NASA officials, Artemis III will be a two-week mission involving four astronauts and a series of docking demonstrations in Earth's orbit, with SpaceX and Blue Origin developing the lunar landers. The mission will not travel to the moon but is designed to test systems and operations needed for future lunar landings.
Artemis III will require multiple launches in quick succession from Florida and give crews an opportunity to conduct docking exercises with both commercial spacecraft, NASA leaders said.
During the briefing, Artemis Program Manager Jeremy Parsons praised SpaceX's rapid development pace.
"We're seeing lots of hardware, lots of quick changes, and an absolute blistering pace of production," he said.
The agency's push comes as China works toward its publicly stated goal of landing astronauts on the moon before 2030, raising concerns among U.S. officials that America could lose momentum in a domain it once dominated.
Isaacman repeatedly invoked the Apollo era, arguing that NASA should draw lessons from when the agency progressed from Apollo 7's first crewed mission to Apollo 11's lunar landing within nine months.
"It's a playbook this agency knows really well, the same playbook that went from Apollo 7 splashdown to Apollo 11 in just nine months," he said.
While emphasizing that NASA will not compromise safety, Isaacman said the agency is working to cut bureaucracy, speed decision-making and increase the pace of hardware development.
The broader goal, he said, extends beyond simply returning astronauts to the moon.
"This will not be a repeat of flags and footprints," Isaacman said.
He described future lunar missions as laying the groundwork for a permanent human presence beyond Earth.
"These vehicles are being designed to dramatically reduce the cost of delivering mass to orbit and to the moon, to support longer surface operations, enable more frequent astronaut missions, and transform what will begin as a small scientific outpost into something that may one day resemble a city on the lunar surface, " Isaacman said.
Newsweek has reached out to the White House and SpaceX for comment.

articles.title_orig: Trump at South Florida rally revives the idea of military intervention in Cuba after Iran
articles.title_zh: Trump at South Florida rally revives the idea of military intervention in Cuba after Iran
articles.content_orig:
US secretary of state makes comments after Trump tells US rally warships could intervene on return from Iran
Marco Rubio urged Cubans seeking political change in their country to act, saying “now is the time” moments after Donald Trump told a Friday rally for candidates in south Florida that US warships could intervene in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war.
The US secretary of state, in his social media post addressed “to those who seek to create positive change”, urged Cubans to capitalize on Trump’s plans. “The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA,” Rubio said.
The top US diplomat, whose parents left Cuba for the United States before the socialist revolution there, seemed to mistakenly use the word “discrete”, meaning separate, rather than “discreet”, meaning private or secret.
Trump first floated this idea earlier this year, but has not mentioned it in recent months. But he revived it in response to a shouted question from the crowd about the island nation. He was campaigning just days before midterm elections in which voters have expressed concern about the impact the US war on Iran has had on prices of goods from gas to groceries.
“We’ll do a little stopover,” Trump said. “Actually, what we’re going to do with Cuba is, we’re going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands. And then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”
Havana on Friday mocked the “desperation” of the US following the comments made by Rubio and Trump.
“Now the United States is resorting to public recruitment for the CIA,” Cuban deputy foreign minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossio wrote on X.
“There must be a great deal of desperation or misery within the agency for it to be forced to sell its services like a tube of toothpaste.”
Rubio and Trump have been bullish on action in Cuba, with Trump previously suggesting the country would “be next” in terms of intervention abroad, following the winding down of the Iran war he has long forecast but which has not yet happened.
In May, he and Rubio raised the specter of US military intervention in Cuba, a renewed threat that took on greater weight after the administration announced criminal charges against the island’s former leader, Raúl Castro. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that previous US presidents had considered intervening in Cuba for decades but that “it looks like I’ll be the one that does it”.
Rubio told reporters separately that Cuba had been a national security threat for years because of its ties to US adversaries and that Trump was intent on addressing it. While saying the Trump administration wanted to resolve differences with Cuba peacefully, Rubio voiced doubts that the US could reach a diplomatic resolution with the island’s current government.
Rubio has not addressed Cuba in depth in public for several weeks, with his last comments coming in a 29 September interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity.
“The truth is Cuba has already fallen. It doesn’t have a functional economy and it’s governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that’s never worked,” Rubio said, without alluding to any CIA operation.
“We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful … that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they’re facing. We’re never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear.”
Rubio and other top Trump aides have met with Cuban officials in recent months to explore possible improvements in relations. But the US side has come away unimpressed from those talks, leading to even more sanctions imposed on the Cuban government.
During his address to the United Nations general assembly last month, Trump said Rubio – son of Cuban immigrants, who has long taken a hard line against Cuba’s socialist leadership – was “deep into negotiations with Cuba”, saying he would “not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep”.
Days later, Trump told reporters that he anticipated that the two countries “will make a deal”, adding: “I don’t think we’ll need the military. Cuba is failing very badly.”
Earlier this week, the two countries clashed at the United Nations as the Trump administration sought once again to build opposition for an upcoming annual vote condemning Washington’s decades-long economic embargo against Havana.
Cuba has struggled since 2020 with an economic and energy crisis. Its gross domestic product has shrunk , and its 10 million residents have endured blackouts, food shortages and inflation. There have been waves of protests, and hundreds of thousands of Cubans have immigrated, many to the United States.

articles.title_orig: China’s AI compute power set to double, but heavily reliant on US chips: report
articles.title_zh: China’s AI compute power set to double, but heavily reliant on US chips: report
articles.content_orig:
China’s remote access alone is expected to swell to 2.8 million H100-equivalents by the end of 2027, up from roughly 1 million this year
China’s access to artificial intelligence computing power will double next year, but US-designed chips will account for about 65 per cent of that capacity, an indication of its continued reliance on foreign hardware, according to new research.
Total compute available to Chinese entities was expected to expand in 2027 from about 4.6 million to 8.8 million “H100-equivalents” – a metric benchmarked against Nvidia’s data-centre graphics processing units, according to a report by the Washington-based Institute for Progress (IFP).
While the US maintains a roughly 16-fold advantage in AI training compute over China, leading Chinese models lag their American rivals by only 6.5 months, the report said.

articles.title_orig: Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya
articles.title_zh: Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya
articles.content_orig:
Kenya has recorded its second death from Ebola as it handles its first ever outbreak of the disease.
A woman, aged 65, who was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, died after being placed in quarantine, the health ministry said.
Seven other Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities, it added.
All the cases were within "one cluster, with no evidence of community spread", the ministry said.
More than 4,000 people have died in Africa since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.
Kenya's latest victim was a "direct contact and close family member of the first case (deceased) and was under quarantine when she developed symptoms" on 13 October, the health ministry said.
The first death, on 5 October, was that of a man who fell ill in September and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo before arriving in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, where he died a few days later.
Those still being treated are three other relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner.
The US has warned its citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.
Ebola is a rare but deadly disease caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The Bundibugyo species of Ebola is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.
Kenya has introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from DR Congo and nine other countries it considers to be at high risk: Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.
Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.
Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.
It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.
In another development, Nigeria's health minister has said the country's single confirmed case of Ebola appears to be genetically related to a strain identified earlier in Kenya.
Professor Ali Pate said there was no evidence so far that the Kenyan patient had travelled to Nigeria, but that further testing was under way.
He emphasised that Nigeria had so far recorded only one confirmed case of the virus.
"We are conducting additional tests. Some of the results are negative, while others are pending," Pate said.
Health officials have been investigating whether Nigeria's first case crossed paths with Kenya's first patient. Both are believed to have travelled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport earlier this month.

articles.title_orig: In U.S. Gas Talks With Kremlin, Hidden Financing for Alaska Project Emerges
articles.title_zh: In U.S. Gas Talks With Kremlin, Hidden Financing for Alaska Project Emerges
articles.content_orig:
High-level representatives from the US and Russia discussed lifting sanctions against Russia's flagship Arctic LNG-2 project in exchange for Novatek's participation in a $25 billion US gas project in Alaska, according to the Financial Times .
Joel Riddle, former CEO of Polar Train LNG, stated that the Russian company Novatek had financed the Alaska gas terminal project and determined its strategic direction even before obtaining the necessary permits from US authorities.
According to him, he left the company in September due to concerns about violating sanctions. Nearly the entire management team, including the CFO, subsequently resigned.
The FT reviewed correspondence in which a top Novatek executive discussed project financing and expediting fund transfers. ​ According to the agency's sources, the project was part of negotiations between Washington and Moscow regarding potential business agreements amid attempts to end the war against Ukraine.
Discussions centered on Novatek's assistance in building the terminal in Alaska in exchange for lifting sanctions on Russia's Arctic LNG-2.
The project was launched with the participation of investor Gentry Beach, who is connected to the Trump family. Following Riddle's departure, Tim Talkington, the former head of Goldman Sachs' Russian division, became acting CEO.
Earlier, US President Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin reached an agreement on the supply of Russian diesel fuel to the global market, signaling a partial lifting of sanctions against Russia.

articles.title_zh: Patient dies in Bristol Myers Squibb autoimmune CAR-T trial
articles.content_orig:
Elaine’s stories explore the boom in new obesity treatments, new drug payment models, the ways companies are affected by FDA changes, and the emerging psychedelics drug sector. She co-writes The Readout newsletter , and co-hosts STAT’s weekly biotech podcast, The Readout Loud . You can reach Elaine on Signal at elaineywchen.70.
Bristol Myers Squibb on Friday reported that one patient died after receiving its investigational CAR-T therapy in an early autoimmune trial, adding to safety concerns about a growing field of research.
In a Phase 1 trial that tested the therapy in multiple sclerosis, a condition that causes muscle weakness and extreme fatigue, the patient experienced motor symptoms that did not resolve with standard autoimmune treatments. They were then given a potent immunosuppressant, but developed septic pneumonia and died, Bristol said in a press release.
In a subsequent statement sent to STAT, Bristol said this patient was treated for a series of other complications prior to receiving the CAR-T therapy, “confounding our ability to determine the root cause of the issue.”

articles.title_orig: MTA suspending bus fare enforcement teams after altercations emerge
articles.title_zh: MTA suspending bus fare enforcement teams after altercations emerge
articles.content_orig:
Make your contribution now and help Gothamist thrive in 2026. Donate today
Gothamist is funded by sponsors and member donations
The MTA is temporarily shutting down its bus fare enforcement teams after a Brooklyn school dean was roughed up by agents who suspected he hadn’t paid , MTA Chair Janno Lieber announced at a news conference Thursday, adding that a second incident had also come to his attention.
The MTA will review safety protocols while the so-called EAGLE teams are taken off the street. Lieber shared few details about the second incident, but said it raised similar questions about whether the agents involved had shared timely, accurate information about the altercation with supervisors.
“I was not happy that leadership of the MTA and even New York City Transit didn’t even hear about that episode until more than a week afterwards. It now appears that there is another episode where that failure to timely report is even more extreme. The incident that's come to attention is now several months old and it didn’t come up,” Lieber said.
“I’m not willing to keep our teams active in the field until I know that all protocols are being followed with respect to both the customer interactions, how they’re conducted, but also with respect to the reporting and investigation of incidents … As a result I’m ordering an immediate safety stand-down until these investigations conclude,” he added.
Lieber has previously said the EAGLE teams, who scan bus tickets and issue fines to fare-beaters, are critical to reducing rampant fare evasion on buses. MTA statistics show as much as half of bus riders skip the fare.
But a video of a confrontation between EAGLE agents and Mott Bridges Academy dean Kyle Taylor prompted questions about the conduct of the teams enforcing $3 rides.
Video showed agents pinned Taylor against a bus and slammed him to the ground after they asked if he paid his fare on a B14 bus in Brownsville. He sustained injuries to his back, neck, shoulder, arm and elbow.
The MTA suspended the agents involved while it began investigating the incident. Taylor maintains he did pay for the fare after transferring from a different bus, where he received a transfer ticket.
An EAGLE officer filed official paperwork reporting that Taylor “fell out of the bus” and refused medical attention, an account contradicted by the video footage.
Taylor’s lawyer Benjamin Pinczewski called for a complete dissolution of the unit. “ It disproportionately subjects people of color to this kind of treatment, and it's unacceptable,” Pinczewski said.
“We’re going to take a break, and take another look and we’ll be back when we’ve completed that,” Lieber added.
Jeremy Edwards, a spokesperson for Mayor Zohran Mamdani, praised the move.
“No New Yorker should fear for their safety because they cannot afford the fare. We welcome the MTA’s decision to suspend fare enforcement while it investigates reports of excessive force by members of its fare collection teams. Our transit system should make life easier, not harder,” Edwards said.
